title: "1. Look at your data"
---

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
- The first commandment of data analysis is look at your data
  - Problems and/or quirks with the data are easily ascertained
  - Modeling strategies often become clear only after examining the data
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](images/look-at-your-data.png){fig-alt="Moses holding a stone tablet that reads: Look at your data!"}
:::
::::

## Histograms

- Histograms have the advantage of being intuitive and widely used
  - Skew is easy to ascertain via a histogram
- Histograms "bin" values within a certain range and plot the quantity within that bin as height: higher bars represent ranges that are more frequent in the data

![](images/mize-2016-histogram.png){width=60% fig-alt="Published histogram: distribution of the log of hourly wages for all employed women in the GSS."}

::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"}
From [Mize (2016)](http://asr.sagepub.com/content/early/2016/10/24/0003122416674025.full.pdf+html)
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/gss.dta", clear
(gss.dta | GSS 1972 - 2016 Data | DMV Workshop)

. 
. // 1.a - freq option to plot # of obs in each bin
. hist wages, freq fcol(none) xlab(0(10)70) ///
>     title("[1.a] Histogram of Distribution of Hourly Wages") ///
>     subtitle("y-axis shows number of observations in bin")
(bin=44, start=.10516854, width=1.5885189)

```

![](fig/dmv-01_a-hist.png){width=80% fig-alt="[1.a] Histogram of hourly wages from 0 to 70 with frequency on the y-axis: the distribution is skewed to the right, with most wages between about 5 and 25 and a small spike at the top value of 70."}

## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(foreign)            # load Stata datasets
library(ggplot2)            # main graphics package
library(dplyr)              # data manipulation tools
library(cleanplots)         # Mize's graphics scheme

## Use cleanplots colors, markers, lines, and theme for all graphs ##
cleanplots_defaults()
theme_update(plot.title.position = "plot")   # titles start at left edge of graph

# General Social Survey Data
gss <- droplevels(read.dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/gss.dta"))

# 1.a - Frequency option to plot # of observations in each bin
ggplot(gss, aes(x = wages)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = NA, color = "gray20") +
  labs(x = "Wages", y = "Frequency",
       title = "[1.a] Histogram of Distribution of Hourly Wages",
       subtitle = "y-axis shows number of observations in bin") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 70, 10))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](1-look-at-your-data_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){fig-alt='[1.a] Histogram of hourly wages from 0 to 70 with frequency on the y-axis: the distribution is skewed to the right, with most wages between about 5 and 25 and a small spike at the top value of 70.' width=80%}
:::
:::


:::

## Kernel density plots

- Kernel density plots provide smoothed lines showing the distribution of a variable
  - Think of these as a smoothed histogram
  - Rather than the height of individual bins at different values showing frequency/percent, the height of the smooth line illustrates density of the data at that value
    - NOTE: density ≈ proportion of observations near that value

![](images/kernel-density-explained.png){width=70% fig-alt="A kernel density curve drawn over a row of individual data points: the curve is highest where the points are most concentrated."}

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. // 1.b - Overlay a kernel density plot on a histogram to illustrate what it do
> es
. *NOTE: Just pedagogical, not a graph you would usually make
. twoway ///
>     hist     wages, fcol(none) || ///
>     kdensity wages, col(red)   || ///
>     , xlab(0(10)70) legend(order(1 "Histogram" 2 "Kernel Density")) ///
>     ytitle("Density") xtitle("Hourly Wages ($)") ///
>     title("[1.b] Distribution of Hourly Wages") ///
>     subtitle("Comparison of histogram and kernel density plot")

```

![](fig/dmv-01_b-hist_kdensity.png){width=80% fig-alt="[1.b] Histogram of hourly wages on the density scale with a red kernel density line overlaid: the smooth line follows the tops of the bars, peaking near 10 dollars and trailing off to the right."}

## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 1.b - Overlay a kernel density plot on a histogram to illustrate what it does
# NOTE: Just pedagogical, not a graph you would usually make
ggplot(gss, aes(x = wages)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), fill = NA, color = "gray20") +
  geom_density(color = cleanplots_colors("red")) +
  labs(x = "Hourly Wages ($)", y = "Density",
       title = "[1.b] Distribution of Hourly Wages",
       subtitle = "Comparison of histogram and kernel density plot") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 70, 10))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](1-look-at-your-data_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-alt='[1.b] Histogram of hourly wages on the density scale with a red kernel density line overlaid: the smooth line follows the tops of the bars, peaking near 10 dollars and trailing off to the right.' width=80%}
:::
:::


:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. // 1.c - Usually, just want the density and not the histogram too
. kdensity wages, xlab(0(10)70) ///
>     ytitle("Density") xtitle("Hourly Wages ($)") ///
>     title("[1.c] Kernel Density Plot of Hourly Wages")

```

![](fig/dmv-01_c-kdensity.png){width=80% fig-alt="[1.c] Kernel density plot of hourly wages: the line rises steeply to a peak near 10 dollars and then declines slowly toward 70."}

## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 1.c - Usually, just want the density and not the histogram too
ggplot(gss, aes(x = wages)) +
  geom_density() +
  labs(x = "Hourly Wages ($)", y = "Density",
       title = "[1.c] Kernel Density Plot of Hourly Wages") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 70, 10))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](1-look-at-your-data_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-alt='[1.c] Kernel density plot of hourly wages: the line rises steeply to a peak near 10 dollars and then declines slowly toward 70.' width=80%}

## Box (and whisker) plots

- Box plots are useful for comparing distributions across variables or across waves (or groups)
  - Standardized rules make comparing distributions easy

![](images/box-plot-example.jpeg){width=60% fig-alt="Example box plots of test scores for four groups, A through D."}

### Box and whisker plot rules

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}
- Rules:
  - Line break in middle of box = median
  - Box boundaries = interquartile range (IQR)
    - IQR: 75^th^ percentile -- 25^th^ percentile
  - Whiskers = range of data without outliers\*
    - I.e., Where the vast majority of the data falls
  - Dots = outliers
    - NOTE: Following [Tukey (1977)](https://books.google.com/books/about/Exploratory_Data_Analysis.html?id=UT9dAAAAIAAJ), the length of the whiskers (and thus, the cutoff for outliers) is:
      1. Upper cutoff: 75^th^ percentile + 1.5 \* IQR
      2. Lower cutoff: 25^th^ percentile - 1.5 \* IQR
:::
::: {.column width="35%"}
![](images/box-plot-rules.png){fig-alt="Diagram of adjacent values and outliers: the quartiles Q1 and Q3, the IQR between them, the upper and lower adjacent values, and the cutoffs Q3 + 1.5 IQR and Q1 - 1.5 IQR."}
:::
::::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/ah_si.dta", clear
(ah-si.dta | Add Health Waves 1-6: Cleaned for MCAP SI)

. 
. * Top code drinks in the past year at 1,000
. gen numdrinksyrT = numdrinksyr
(432 missing values generated)

. recode numdrinksyrT 1000 / 9125 = 1000
(1,649 changes made to numdrinksyrT)

. lab var numdrinksyrT "# of drinks last year (top coded at 1,000)"

. 
. // 1.d - Drinks in the past year, with separate boxes by wave
. graph box numdrinksyrT, over(wave) ///
>     ytitle("# of drinks in the past year") ///
>     title("[1.d] Box plot of drinks in the past year by wave of Add Health") /
> //
>     subtitle("Top coded at 1,000 drinks")

```

![](fig/dmv-01_d-boxplot.png){width=80% fig-alt="[1.d] Box plots of the number of drinks in the past year for Add Health waves 1 to 6: waves 1 and 2 have very small boxes near zero, waves 3 and 4 have the widest boxes, and every wave has many outliers up to the top code of 1,000."}

## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Add Health Data
ah <- read.dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/ah_si.dta")

# Top code drinks in the past year at 1,000
ah$numdrinksyrT <- pmin(ah$numdrinksyr, 1000)

# 1.d - Drinks in the past year, with separate boxes by wave
ggplot(ah, aes(x = wave, y = numdrinksyrT)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "",
       y = "# of drinks in the past year",
       title = "[1.d] Box plot of drinks in the past year by wave of Add Health",
       subtitle = "Top coded at 1,000 drinks")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](1-look-at-your-data_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-alt='[1.d] Box plots of the number of drinks in the past year for Add Health waves 1 to 6: waves 1 and 2 have very small boxes near zero, waves 3 and 4 have the widest boxes, and every wave has many outliers up to the top code of 1,000.' width=80%}
:::
:::


:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. // 1.e - Add a second grouping variable
. graph box numdrinksyrT, ///
>     over(male) over(wave) asyvars horizontal ///
>     ytitle("# of drinks in the past year") ///
>     title("[1.e] Box plot of drinks in the past year by Add Health wave and ge
> nder") ///
>     subtitle("Top coded at 1,000 drinks")

```

![](fig/dmv-01_e-boxplot_by_gender.png){width=80% fig-alt="[1.e] Horizontal box plots of drinks in the past year by Add Health wave, with separate red boxes for females and light blue boxes for males: the female boxes are wider in waves 3 and 4 and the male boxes are wider in waves 5 and 6."}

## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 1.e - Add a second grouping variable
ggplot(filter(ah, !is.na(male)), aes(x = wave, y = numdrinksyrT, fill = male)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "",
       y = "# of drinks in the past year", fill = "",
       title = "[1.e] Box plot of drinks in the past year by Add Health wave and gender",
       subtitle = "Top coded at 1,000 drinks")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](1-look-at-your-data_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-alt='[1.e] Horizontal box plots of drinks in the past year by Add Health wave, with separate red boxes for females and light blue boxes for males: the female boxes are wider in waves 3 and 4 and the male boxes are wider in waves 5 and 6.' width=80%}
